0: Generative artificial intelligence (AIGC) has been an important direction in AI in recent years. Unlike traditional classification, prediction and retrieval tasks, a generative model's goal is to learn the probability distribution of the data and generate new content guided by conditions such as text or images.
1: From the early generative adversarial networks (GAN) and variational autoencoders (VAE) to the diffusion models and Diffusion Transformers (DiT) widely used in recent years, generative models keep improving in generation quality, training stability, semantic understanding and inference efficiency. On that basis, text-to-image models such as Stable Diffusion, FLUX, Qwen-Image and Z-Image have further pushed AIGC into content creation, advertising design and marketing asset production.
3: The core goal of a generative model is to learn the probability distribution underlying the training data and its internal patterns, and to generate new samples matching that distribution under given conditions. Unlike classification or retrieval, a generative model does not pick one answer from a predefined candidate set; it uses the data patterns it has learned to generate new text, images, audio or video.
4: From a probabilistic modelling point of view, conditional generation can be written as \(p(x \mid c)\): the conditional probability distribution of generating content x given condition c. The condition c is, for example, the user's prompt, the context, a reference image or other control information; x is the target content to generate. Training is essentially learning, under different conditions, the probability of each possible result; inference is producing a concrete result on the basis of that probability distribution.
5: Although large language models, image generation models and video generation models are all generative models, the way they generate is not exactly the same.
6: Take a large language model: today's mainstream models generate text autoregressively. Given the existing context, the model predicts the probability distribution of the next Token, selects or samples the next Token from it, adds the new Token to the context and continues predicting the following Tokens. By repeating this process it eventually forms the complete text.
7: Image generation models use a different mechanism. In a diffusion model, for example, generation usually starts from random noise and gradually denoises it under the guidance of conditions such as the text prompt, so the noise gradually forms an image with clear structure and semantics. Whether autoregression, diffusion or another mechanism is used, the common goal is the same: learn the distribution of real data and generate new content that follows those patterns under given conditions.
8: One important reason a generative model can produce new content is that what it learns is not one particular text or image but the statistical relations and feature patterns among a large amount of training data.
9: After learning many beverage advertising images, for example, the model may build up associations between visual concepts such as the bottle, ice cubes, splashes, fruit, background colour, lighting and commercial photography style. Given “summer lime drink commercial advertisement” as input, the model can reorganise these visual elements according to the learned patterns to form a new image. “Generation” does not mean looking up an existing item in the training set; it means modelling and combining different features and concepts according to the learned data distribution.
10: Another important characteristic of generative models is the diversity of their output. For the same prompt, “a cat sitting by the window”, the model may generate cats of different breeds, poses and fur colours, and may use different lighting, backgrounds and framing. These results all match the input semantically, yet their concrete content is not identical. The reason is that the prompt only imposes a certain constraint on the generated content rather than fully specifying the final result. Under a given condition there are usually several reasonable outcomes in the distribution the model has learned. In actual generation, factors such as the sampling strategy and the random seed further influence the output. Unlike traditional tasks with a definite answer, a generation task usually has no single optimal output: one input condition can correspond to several reasonable results.
12: Text generation plays a fundamental role in the development of modern generative AI. On one hand, large language models drove the rapid spread of AIGC technology; on the other, concepts such as Tokenizer, Embedding, Transformer, probability distribution and sampling apply not only to text generation but also recur in text-to-image and multimodal generation later. In today's AIGC systems in particular, the text prompt has become an important way for users to control the generated content. Whether generating a passage of text, an image or a video, the model usually has to understand the user's natural language first.
14: Natural language cannot take part in neural network computation directly. Before text enters the model it must first be split by a Tokenizer and converted into Token IDs. A Token is the basic unit a language model uses to process text: it may be one Chinese character, a complete word, or part of a word, and the exact split is decided by the tokenisation algorithm and vocabulary the model uses. A Token ID is essentially just the Token's index in the vocabulary, and its numeric value does not indicate the semantic relation between Tokens. Two Tokens with close IDs, for example, are not necessarily semantically similar. So before entering the neural network for computation, the discrete Token IDs must be mapped by an Embedding layer into continuous high-dimensional vectors; this idea of representing language with continuous vectors is an important foundation of modern natural language processing. In 2013 Mikolov et al. proposed Word2Vec, which learns distributed vector representations of words from large corpora through a neural network. Its basic idea comes from the distributional hypothesis in natural language: words appearing in similar contexts usually have similar semantic or grammatical features.
15: Word2Vec mainly contains two training structures: CBOW (Continuous Bag-of-Words) and Skip-gram. Both learn word vectors from the relation between a centre word and its context words, but the prediction direction differs.
16: CBOW predicts the centre word from the context words. For a sequence of words, first pick a centre word and take the words within a certain window around it as the context. The model uses the vector representations of these context words to predict the centre word. For instance, take “eat” as the centre word and choose the surrounding “like” and “fresh” as context.
17: Skip-gram predicts the surrounding context words from the centre word. Compared with CBOW its prediction direction is reversed. For the same word sequence, when “eat” is the centre word, Skip-gram's training goal is to predict other words that may appear within a certain window from the vector representation of “eat”, such as “like” and “fresh”. The main difference between CBOW and Skip-gram is the training goal: CBOW uses several context words to predict one centre word, while Skip-gram uses one centre word to predict several context words. Despite the different directions, both ultimately learn word vectors from the many co-occurrence relations between words. Once trained, each word can be represented as a fixed-dimension continuous vector.
18: Word2Vec drove the development of distributed word representation, but its representation still has limitations. What Word2Vec learns is a typical static word embedding: once trained, a word usually corresponds to a fixed vector that does not change with the specific context. Modern language models go further and use contextual representation. A Token first gets an initial vector from the Embedding layer, then passes through several neural network layers that keep updating its representation from information about other Tokens in the sequence. The same Token can therefore form different hidden states in different contexts, expressing meaning related to the current context. Word2Vec's significance lies not only in proposing a concrete word-vector training method but in driving the wide use of distributed representation in natural language processing. Language is no longer represented only by discrete symbols or IDs but is also mapped into a continuous vector space, letting neural networks learn the semantic and grammatical relations between words. Later work in natural language processing paid further attention to adjusting word representations dynamically with context.
20: In 2017 the Transformer architecture was proposed. Transformer models the relations between different positions in a sequence through the attention mechanism and gradually became the core base architecture of large language models. One of its most important mechanisms is Self-Attention, as shown below:
21: The main role of self-attention is to let the model consider the information contained in other Tokens of the sequence when processing one Token, and to assign different attention weights dynamically according to how strongly they relate. Specifically, each Token's representation is mapped into Query (Q), Key (K) and Value (V). The model computes attention weights from how well the Query matches different Keys, then uses those weights to combine the corresponding Values into a new representation that has fused the context information.
22: Transformer is usually built by stacking several network layers. In different layers the model keeps updating each Token's representation so that it gradually fuses richer context. After several Transformer layers, the same Token can form different contextual representations in different contexts, supporting the model's ability to model word meaning, syntactic structure and more complex semantic relations. Transformer's significance lies not only in introducing a new network structure but in providing a mechanism that models context relations effectively. Modern large language models build on Transformer and keep improving language understanding and generation by scaling model size, training data and context length.
24: After the Transformer has modelled the context of the input sequence, the language model already has Token representations that include context information. On that basis a generative language model must further predict what comes next. Mainstream generative large language models such as GPT usually generate autoregressively: from the Tokens already input or generated, they predict and generate subsequent Tokens step by step.
25: For a sequence made of several Tokens, the generation probability can be decomposed into a series of conditional probabilities:
26: \(p(x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_T) = \prod_{t=1}^{T} p(x_t \mid x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_{t-1}) \)
27: Where \(x_t\) is the t-th Token to generate and \(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_{t-1}\) are the Tokens already input or generated. The formula shows that generating a complete text sequence can be decomposed into a series of consecutive next-Token predictions.
28: After computing the probability distribution over the next Token, the model still needs a decoding strategy to decide the Token actually output. Different decoding strategies directly affect the stability, diversity and creativity of the generated text.
29: The most direct way is greedy decoding, choosing the highest-probability Token at every step. It is strongly deterministic, but always taking the locally most probable Token does not necessarily give the best text overall, and the output tends to become monotonous. To increase diversity, generative language models can also use random sampling, choosing the next Token according to the predicted probability distribution. Higher-probability Tokens are more likely to be chosen, but other reasonable candidates also have a chance. In practice, methods such as Temperature, Top-k and Top-p are usually combined to adjust the sampling process further.
30: Temperature adjusts how smooth the probability distribution is; it can be written as:
32: Where \(z_i\) is the Logit for the i-th Token, i.e. the raw score the model computes for each candidate Token before Softmax, and \(T\) is the Temperature.
33: When \(T\) is small, the advantage of high-probability Tokens is further reinforced and the model tends to pick the more probable results, so the output is usually more stable; when \(T\) is large, the distribution is flatter and low-probability Tokens get more chances, so the output is usually more diverse.
34: Top-k keeps only the \(k\) most probable candidate Tokens at each generation step and samples after renormalising the probabilities among them. It filters out many low-probability Tokens and reduces the chance of clearly unreasonable content being chosen.
35: Top-p does not fix the number of candidates: it orders Tokens by probability from high to low, takes the smallest candidate set whose cumulative probability reaches the threshold \(p\) and samples from that set. Top-p can therefore adjust the candidate range dynamically according to the current distribution.
36: For example, when the model is fairly certain about the next Token, a few Tokens already reach the threshold; when there are several reasonable candidates, more Tokens are kept for sampling. Text generation actually contains two closely linked processes: first the language model computes the probability distribution of the next Token from the context, then the decoding and sampling strategy decides the Token actually generated from that distribution.
37: The model learns which Tokens are more likely in the current context, while the decoding strategy decides how to pick a concrete result among those candidates. Together they determine the accuracy, stability and diversity of the final text.
39: In the development of deep generative models, the generative adversarial network (GAN) is a representative technique. In 2014 Goodfellow et al. proposed GAN, which learns the distribution of real data through adversarial training between two neural networks. Unlike traditional supervised learning, GAN does not directly specify what image the generator should output: it also introduces a discriminator to evaluate the generated result and uses that evaluation to keep improving the generator. After it appeared, GAN was quickly applied to image generation, face generation, image style transfer, super-resolution and image editing, producing a series of representative models such as CycleGAN, StyleGAN and ESRGAN.
41: GAN learns the distribution of real data through adversarial training between two neural networks, a Generator and a Discriminator. As shown in the figure, during training the discriminator receives both real samples from the training set and generated samples produced by the generator and tells the two apart; the generator keeps adjusting its parameters from the feedback the discriminator provides, increasing the similarity between generated and real samples.
42: The generator is written G. Its input is usually a random variable z sampled from some simple probability distribution, such as a Gaussian or uniform distribution. After the generator's non-linear mapping, the random variable is turned into a generated sample:
44: In image generation, the generator's goal is to map a low- or high-dimensional random representation step by step into an image with a particular visual structure.
45: The discriminator is written D. Its input includes real samples x from the training set and samples G(z) produced by the generator. By learning the feature differences between the two kinds of data, the discriminator outputs the probability that the input sample comes from the real data distribution:
47: For real samples the discriminator wants the output near 1; for generated samples it wants the output near 0. The generator and discriminator have opposite optimisation goals. The discriminator must keep improving its ability to tell real from generated samples, while the generator must keep improving the realism of its samples so that they come closer to real samples in data features. The two networks form an adversarial relation as they are optimised alternately. The original paper defines the GAN training objective as a minimax game:
48: \(\min_G \max_D V(D,G) = \mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{\mathrm{data}}(x)} [\log D(x)] + \mathbb{E}_{z\sim p_z(z)} [\log(1-D(G(z)))] \)
49: Where \(p_{\mathrm{data}}\) is the real data distribution and \(p_z\) the prior distribution of the random variable. The discriminator \(D\) maximises the objective to improve its ability to tell real from generated samples; the generator \(G\) optimises its own parameters so the generated distribution approaches the real data distribution.
50: GAN training usually uses alternating optimisation. First the discriminator \(D\) is updated with real and generated samples so it learns the differences between the two kinds of data; then the generator \(G\) is updated using the gradient information the discriminator produces, so it gradually improves its results. As training continues, the abilities of the generator and discriminator both change, forming a dynamic adversarial learning process.
51: The generator and discriminator play different roles in GAN. The discriminator is mainly used during training, giving the generator an optimisation signal through real/fake classification; once training is done, if the task is only to generate new images, the generator alone is enough for inference:
53: GAN attracts wide attention in image generation largely because its generation process is fairly direct. Once trained, you only need to feed a random variable into the generator and one forward pass gives the result. Compared with models that need many iterative steps, GAN is usually more efficient, and it is therefore widely used in image generation, super-resolution, video enhancement and interactive image processing. GAN's advantage lies mainly in the generation stage; its training is relatively complex, with the following main problems.
55: GAN must train a generator and a discriminator at the same time, and the two networks have opposing optimisation goals. When the generator's parameters change, the generated data the discriminator faces changes too; when the discriminator's parameters change, the optimisation signal the generator receives changes too. So, unlike ordinary supervised learning optimised against a relatively fixed objective, GAN training is in fact a dynamic game that keeps changing. If the discriminator is too strong, generated samples are easily identified and the generator struggles to get an effective optimisation signal; if it is too weak, it cannot accurately reflect the difference between real and generated samples and likewise fails to give the generator useful feedback. Keeping training relatively stable between generator and discriminator is therefore an important problem in GAN training.
57: Mode collapse is another typical problem in GAN training. Ideally the generator should not only produce samples of high visual quality but also cover the different types and features in the real data. If the training data contains faces of different ages, expressions and appearance, for example, the generator should produce correspondingly diverse faces. In real training, however, the generator may tend to produce a few kinds of samples that more easily earn a high discriminator score and keep generating similar results. A single generated image may then be of high quality, but the many results differ little and do not cover the diversity of the real data. Mode collapse reflects an important point about generative models: high quality on a single sample does not mean the model has fully learned the real data distribution.
58: To address training instability, mode collapse and generation quality, researchers improved GAN in network structure, loss functions and training strategies, producing many derived models. This work not only improved GAN's generation ability but gradually extended it from basic image generation to image translation, controllable image editing and image super-resolution. A few representative models illustrate typical GAN applications in these directions.
60: As GAN technology developed, its applications gradually extended from random image generation to image translation, image editing and image enhancement. Different models usually redesign the generator, discriminator, loss function or training method for a specific task, forming GAN variants with different functions. CycleGAN, DragGAN, ESRGAN and Real-ESRGAN represent typical GAN applications in unpaired image translation, interactive image editing and image super-resolution respectively.
62: In 2017 Zhu et al. proposed CycleGAN, mainly to solve the unpaired image-to-image translation problem. Unlike translation methods that need paired training samples, CycleGAN does not require a one-to-one correspondence between source and target images: you only need to provide data from each of the two image domains and it learns the mapping between them. In the horse-to-zebra task, for example, traditional methods usually need corresponding horse and zebra images, whereas CycleGAN only needs a set of horse images and a set of zebra images, with no correspondence between them. As shown below, CycleGAN consists of two generators and two discriminators and learns translation in both directions at once. Suppose horse images belong to image domain \(X\) and zebra images to domain \(Y\); generator \(G\) translates from \(X\) to \(Y\) and generator \(F\) translates from \(Y\) to \(X\):
64: Where discriminator \(D_Y\) judges whether generated zebra images match the real zebra distribution and discriminator \(D_X\) judges whether generated horse images match the real horse distribution. CycleGAN therefore actually contains adversarial learning in two directions:
65: \( G + D_Y:\quad X \rightarrow Y \qquad \text{(horse} \rightarrow \text{zebra)} \)
66: \( F + D_X:\quad Y \rightarrow X \qquad \text{(zebra} \rightarrow \text{horse)} \)
67: Adversarial training in the two directions alone cannot guarantee that the translated image still corresponds to the original input. When converting a horse image into a zebra, for example, the result may have realistic zebra texture while the horse's pose, position or background structure changes greatly. Content consistency before and after translation is not sufficiently guaranteed.
68: So CycleGAN further introduces a cycle consistency constraint. As the lower part of the figure shows, for a horse image \(x\) in domain \(X\), generator \(G\) first converts it into a zebra image \(G(x)\), and generator \(F\) then converts it back into a horse image:
70: After one complete forward and backward translation, the final result should be as close as possible to the original image:
72: Similarly, for a zebra image \(y\) in domain \(Y\), we need:
74: The model therefore forms two complete translation cycles: horse → zebra → horse, and zebra → horse → zebra. To constrain the two cycles, CycleGAN introduces a cycle consistency loss:
76: Where the first term constrains the horse → zebra → horse reconstruction and the second the zebra → horse → zebra reconstruction. The smaller the cycle consistency loss, the closer the image is to the original in content and structure after the two-way translation. CycleGAN training mainly contains adversarial learning and the cycle consistency constraint; together they let CycleGAN learn the mapping between two image domains without paired training data, enabling tasks such as horse-zebra translation and image style transfer.
78: In 2023 Pan et al. proposed DragGAN, which adjusts the position, pose and shape of objects in a generated image interactively by setting handle points and target points. Unlike traditional pixel-level editing, DragGAN does not move pixels in the image directly; it adjusts the GAN's latent representation so the generated image changes in the direction the user specifies.
79: DragGAN's core process mainly consists of motion supervision and point tracking. The user first picks the handle points to adjust in the image and specifies where they should move. In the figure, for example, setting a handle point and a target point near the lion's mouth makes the mouth gradually open.
80: While editing, DragGAN keeps the pretrained generator's parameters fixed and keeps optimising the latent code \(w\) fed to the generator. The initial image can be written as \(I = G(w) \), where \(G\) is the pretrained GAN generator and \(w\) is the latent code for the image. Adjusting \(w\) changes the content and structure of the generated image \(I\). Motion supervision pushes the image features near the handle point towards the target position. After one optimisation the latent code goes from \(w\) to \(w'\) and the generated image changes accordingly. Because the original handle point position may have shifted once the image changes, DragGAN must also use point tracking to re-determine the handle point's position in the new image before the next optimisation round — that is, set handle and target points → motion supervision → optimise the latent code → generate a new image → track points and update the handle points → keep optimising until close to the target position. After several iterations the handle points gradually move to the position the user specified, giving the edited image. Because this process optimises inside the generative space the GAN learned, the model does not only change the specified spot but can adjust related surrounding structure accordingly.
81: The key to DragGAN is not simply dragging pixels; it converts the user's drag into iterative optimisation of the GAN's latent representation and uses motion supervision and point tracking to move the semantic structure in the image towards the specified position. This method shows GAN's ability in controllable image editing, letting users adjust visual attributes such as pose, expression and shape through fairly intuitive point operations.
83: Image super-resolution (SR) is one of the typical GAN applications: generating an image with higher resolution and richer visual detail from a low-resolution one. Unlike simple interpolation upscaling, a super-resolution model must reconstruct the missing high-frequency texture and local structure from the existing image content. In 2018 Wang et al. proposed ESRGAN, further improving the network structure, adversarial loss and perceptual loss on top of earlier work to improve the texture and visual quality of super-resolved images.
84: An important structural improvement in ESRGAN is the Residual-in-Residual Dense Block (RRDB). SRGAN's generator mainly used ordinary residual blocks (Residual Block, RB) containing convolution layers, batch normalisation (Batch Normalization, BN) and an activation function. ESRGAN first removes the BN layers from the residual blocks and further combines several densely connected modules into an RRDB.
85: As the figure shows, an RRDB consists of several Dense Blocks and combines dense connections with residual connections. Inside a Dense Block, different convolution layers are densely connected and later layers can receive and use features extracted by several earlier layers; between Dense Blocks and outside the RRDB, features are further passed through residual connections. This structure strengthens information transfer and feature reuse between layers and improves the network's ability to model image texture and detail features. Besides the structural changes, ESRGAN also optimises the training objective. If a traditional super-resolution method trains mainly on pixel-level error, the model tends to produce fairly smooth results: the pixel error may be small, but some edges and high-frequency texture look blurry. ESRGAN adds perceptual loss and adversarial training so the result keeps the overall content while gaining clearer, more natural texture detail.
86: Generative super-resolution is not the same as recovering information that has been lost. When part of the high-frequency information in a low-resolution image is gone, the existing pixels usually cannot uniquely determine the original detail. ESRGAN in fact combines the input image with image priors learned during training to generate visually plausible texture. The result may look sharper, but some of the detail is not necessarily identical to the original high-resolution image. This makes ESRGAN better suited to image enhancement tasks that emphasise visual quality. In medical imaging, archival forensics and scientific imagery, where information authenticity matters more, generative super-resolution results should be used with care.
88: GAN learns the real data distribution through adversarial training between a generator and a discriminator, while the variational autoencoder (VAE) takes another generative approach: encode the input data into a continuous latent space, sample from that latent space, and generate or reconstruct data through a decoder. In 2013 Kingma and Welling proposed the Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes (AEVB) method and gave the VAE training framework that later became widespread. VAE combines neural networks with variational inference, letting the model learn a latent representation with probabilistic structure through end-to-end training.
90: VAE's basic structure consists of an encoder and a decoder. The encoder compresses the input data into a lower-dimensional latent space and the decoder recovers the input from the latent representation. An ordinary autoencoder usually encodes the input \(x\) directly into a definite latent vector \(z\) and reconstructs with the decoder. VAE's biggest difference is that the encoder does not output a definite latent vector directly but the parameters of a probability distribution over the latent variable.
91: In the figure above, VAE's encoder does not convert the input data \(x\) directly into one fixed latent vector; it also outputs two parameters: the mean \(\mu\) and the standard deviation \(\sigma\). Together they determine the probability distribution of the latent variable \(z\). \(\mu\) fixes roughly where the latent variable sits and \(\sigma\) says how much it can vary around that position.
92: VAE models the latent variable as a Gaussian distribution:
93: \(q_{\phi}(z\mid x) = \mathcal{N} \left( z;\mu_{\phi}(x), \operatorname{diag}\left(\sigma_{\phi}^{2}(x)\right) \right) \)where \(q_{\phi}(z\mid x)\) is the latent variable distribution the encoder obtains from the input \(x\). Unlike an ordinary autoencoder, which gets one definite \(z\), VAE gets a distribution it can sample from, so the same input can yield different latent representations within a range. Next the model must draw a concrete latent variable \(z\) from this distribution and send it to the decoder. To introduce randomness while still allowing backpropagation, VAE uses the reparameterisation trick. The model first samples a random variable \(\epsilon\) from a standard normal distribution and then combines the \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\) from the encoder to compute the latent variable \(z\):
95: It can be understood as: \(\mu\) fixes the position, \(\sigma\) the range of variation and \(\epsilon\) provides randomness; together they give the final latent variable \(z\). This treatment separates random sampling from the computation of network parameters so gradients can still pass through \(z\) to the encoder, enabling end-to-end training of the whole VAE. After the latent variable \(z\) is obtained, the decoder generates the reconstruction \(\hat{x}\) from it. The whole VAE process can be summarised as: input data → encoder → latent distribution → sample \(z\) → decoder → reconstructed data.
96: During training VAE must consider two objectives at once: on one hand the decoder's output should be as close as possible to the original input; on the other the latent distributions for different inputs should not be too scattered but form a relatively continuous, regular latent space. VAE's training objective therefore consists of a reconstruction term and a KL divergence term, usually expressed through the Evidence Lower Bound (ELBO):
97: \(\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ELBO}} = \mathbb{E}_{q_{\phi}(z\mid x)} \left[ \log p_{\theta}(x\mid z) \right] - D_{\mathrm{KL}} \left( q_{\phi}(z\mid x) \parallel p(z) \right) \)
98: Where the first term can be understood as how well reconstruction works, measuring whether the decoder can recover the input from \(z\); the second can be understood as whether the latent space is regular enough, using KL divergence to constrain the latent distribution the encoder produces towards a predefined prior. Both objectives must work together. If only reconstruction mattered, the model could recover the input well but the latent space might be scattered, inconvenient for direct random sampling; with the KL divergence constraint the latent representations of different samples are pulled towards a common prior, making the latent space more regular and better suited to sampling and generation.
100: Looking at the generation process, VAE already has full generative ability. Once trained, you can stop feeding the original image and instead sample a latent variable \(z\) directly from a standard normal distribution, then feed \(z\) into the decoder to generate a new image. Theoretically this works because during training KL divergence keeps constraining the latent distribution the encoder produces towards a predefined standard normal distribution. In real training, though, that latent distribution is usually hard to make exactly match a standard normal. If the constraint is too strong the latent space becomes more regular but part of the image information may be lost; if too weak the latent space may be irregular, so a \(z\) sampled directly from a standard normal can land in a region the model does not know well and degrade the decoding result.
101: At the same time VAE must balance reconstruction quality against latent-space regularity. The classic VAE objective emphasises modelling the overall data distribution and the latent space, and image generation easily loses some high-frequency texture and local detail, so results tend to look smooth. This is a clear difference from GAN in image generation quality. GAN constrains the realism of generated images directly through the discriminator and usually produces sharper texture; VAE focuses more on the continuity and probabilistic structure of the latent space and is somewhat limited in generating high-quality images directly.
103: As generative models developed, VAE's role gradually shifted from generating the final image directly to being a tool for encoding and decoding between image space and latent space. One representative application is the Latent Diffusion Model (LDM). Early diffusion models added and removed noise directly in pixel space. At high image resolution the model must repeatedly process a large number of pixels, which is costly. The latent diffusion model proposed by Rombach et al. moves the diffusion process into a compressed latent space, lowering the data dimension the diffusion model must handle. In this structure an encoder first compresses the original image into a latent representation: original image → Encoder → latent representation. These latent representations no longer store every pixel but keep the main structure and visual information of the image in a more compact form. The diffusion model then adds and removes noise in this latent space instead of handling the original high-resolution image directly. When the diffusion model finishes generating, a decoder restores the generated latent representation to pixel space: generated latent representation → Decoder → final image. VAE compresses and restores the image and the diffusion model generates image content in the latent space. This makes full use of VAE's latent representation ability. What the diffusion model handles is no longer high-dimensional raw pixels but compressed image features, which markedly lowers the computation of the later diffusion and denoising process.
104: VAE itself is somewhat limited in generating high-quality images directly, but its encoder, latent space and decoder structure have become an important part of modern latent diffusion models. This also reflects the change in VAE's role: from an independent generative model it gradually became the latent representation module in high-quality image generation systems.
106: GAN usually generates an image with one forward pass through the generator, and VAE can also start from a latent variable and get a result directly through the decoder. For complex high-dimensional images, making the model map a random variable to a complete image in one go is not easy. Diffusion models take a different approach: they split the complex image generation task into several relatively simple steps, each adjusting the current result only slightly, and reach the complete image after many iterations. They do not require the model to produce the final result in one step but complete generation gradually through repeated denoising.
108: A diffusion model mainly contains two opposite processes: forward diffusion and reverse denoising. Forward diffusion starts from real data \(x_0\) and keeps adding a little random noise. As the time step \(t\) grows, the original information in the image gradually decreases and the noise increases, approaching random Gaussian noise: real image → a little noise → more noise → ... → random noise. In the classic DDPM you can construct noisy data at any time step directly from the original data \(x_0\):
110: Where \(x_0\) is the original data, \(\epsilon\) the random noise sampled from a standard Gaussian, i.e. \(\epsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,I)\), and \(\bar{\alpha}_t\) controls the proportion of original data and noise at the current time step. The later the time step, the less original information and the more noise. Different time steps correspond to different noise levels, and how those levels change is decided by the noise schedule.
111: Forward diffusion itself does not need the model to learn anything: during training you can construct data at different noise levels directly by a predefined rule. What the model really needs to learn is the opposite process, gradually recovering clearer data from noisy data. At generation time the model starts from random noise and denoises only a certain amount at each step: random noise → initial structure → outline gradually sharpens → texture gradually forms → final image. This mechanism splits a complex one-shot generation task into several relatively simple local corrections. The model does not have to predict a complete image at once but keeps adjusting from the current state, which is one important reason diffusion models can generate high quality.
113: The classic DDPM (Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Model) sets up two opposite processes: the forward diffusion process keeps adding noise to real data, while the reverse generation process learns how to remove noise step by step so that random noise eventually becomes an image with the features of real data.
114: \(x_0\) is the real image; as forward diffusion keeps adding Gaussian noise the data passes through \(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_T\) and finally \(x_T\) approaches random Gaussian noise. The dashed line \(q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})\) in the figure is the forward diffusion process, while \(p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\) is the reverse generation process the model must learn. The forward process can be read as \(x_0 \rightarrow x_1 \rightarrow x_2 \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow x_t \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow x_T\), i.e. turning a real image gradually into random noise; generating an image goes in the opposite direction, \(x_T \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow x_t \rightarrow x_{t-1} \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow x_0\), i.e. recovering the final image gradually from random noise. DDPM's key question is how to make the model learn to get a less noisy \(x_{t-1}\) from the current \(x_t\).
115: In DDPM the reverse process is parameterised by a neural network. One important and common implementation is to have the network predict the noise added into \(x_t\). During training, starting from the real image \(x_0\), randomly pick a time step \(t\) and sample Gaussian noise \(\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I) \); from the forward diffusion process you can construct the noisy image for time step \(t\) directly:
116: The noisy image \(x_t\) and the time step \(t\) are then fed into the neural network, which predicts the noise \(\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t) \), where \(\theta\) are the network's parameters. Because the noise actually added during training, \(\epsilon\), is known, you can compare the predicted noise directly with the real one. DDPM training can be understood as actively adding different amounts of noise to real images and then training the model to recognise which noise was added. After plenty of training the model can handle data at different time steps and noise levels and use its noise prediction to construct the reverse process \(p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)\) shown in the figure. At generation time no real image is needed: the process starts directly from Gaussian noise, the model first gets a less noisy \(x_{T-1}\) from \(x_T\), then \(x_{T-2}\) from \(x_{T-1}\), and so on. \(x_T \rightarrow x_{T-1} \rightarrow x_{T-2} \rightarrow \cdots \rightarrow x_1 \rightarrow x_0 \)
117: As the reverse process goes on, the overall structure, outline and texture of an image gradually appear in the random noise, giving the complete generated image. DDPM does not have the model predict a whole image from noise in one go; it learns denoising at several noise levels and completes generation through several reverse iterations. This lowers the difficulty of a single generation step and avoids the adversarial training between generator and discriminator in GAN. However, multi-step sampling means generating one image requires several neural network inferences, so slow inference became one of the main limitations of the classic DDPM.
119: DDPM describes image generation as a step-by-step denoising process: during training it adds noise to real data and has the model learn to predict the noise; at generation time it starts from random noise and gradually obtains an image through several reverse denoising steps. Flow Matching uses a different description. It constructs a continuous probability path between the random noise distribution and the real data distribution and trains the model to learn the direction of change along that path, so random noise can gradually turn into real data along the learned direction.
120: In implementation Flow Matching mainly has three stages: path construction, velocity field learning and generation sampling.
122: During training, first sample an example \(x_0\) from the real data distribution and random noise \(\epsilon\) from a standard Gaussian. To link real data and random noise you can construct a series of continuous intermediate states between them. A fairly intuitive way is linear interpolation:
123: \(x_t=(1-\sigma_t)x_0+\sigma_t\epsilon \)where \(\sigma_t\) controls the proportion of real data and random noise in the current state. For clarity we can set:
124: \(\sigma_0=0,\qquad \sigma_1=1 \)When \(\sigma_t=0\): \(x_t=x_0 \), corresponding to real data; when \(\sigma_t=1\): \(x_t=\epsilon \), corresponding to random noise.
125: As \(\sigma_t\) grows from 0 to 1, \(x_t\) can represent a series of continuous intermediate states between real data and random noise: real data → a little noise → medium noise → a lot of noise → random noise. By randomly choosing different \(t\) during training you get intermediate states at different positions, giving the model training samples to learn how the data changes along the whole path. Compared with DDPM's predefined step-by-step noising, Flow Matching cares more about how to define a continuous path connecting the two distributions and how data should change along it.
126: 2) Learn the velocity field along the path
127: Once the continuous path is built, the next step is to determine the direction and speed of the data's change along the path. Flow Matching uses a neural network to learn a velocity field \(v_\theta(x_t,t) \), where \(x_t\) is the current intermediate state, \(t\) the current time position and \(v_\theta(x_t,t)\) the rate of change the model predicts for the current position. For the linear path above:
129: During training you can obtain the target velocity from the known real data \(x_0\) and random noise \(\epsilon\) and train the network to predict it from the current state \(x_t\) and time \(t\). Flow Matching's training objective is exactly that: given an intermediate state \(x_t\) and time \(t\) on the path, train the model to predict the rate at which the data changes at that position. After learning from many training samples, the velocities at different positions together form a velocity field. This field describes how the data should change at different positions in data space and so provides direction for later generating data from random noise.
130: 3) Generate data along the velocity field
131: The training stage built a path between real data and random noise and learned the velocity field along it. The generation stage starts from random noise and uses the learned velocity field to move gradually towards the real data distribution. This can be expressed as: random noise → intermediate state → data structure gradually forms → final generated data, \(x_{t-1} = x_t+ (\sigma_{t-1}-\sigma_t) v_\theta(x_t,t) \)the model re-predicts the velocity from the current state at each time step and updates \(x_t\). After several iterations the initial random noise gradually turns into generated data with complete structure and semantic information.
132: In terms of modelling, DDPM and Flow Matching both start generation from a simple random distribution, but they describe the generation process differently. DDPM describes data change mainly through forward diffusion and reverse denoising and usually learns noise prediction; Flow Matching constructs a continuous path linking noise and real data, learns the velocity field along that path, and then generates data step by step along the velocity field starting from random noise.
134: Text-to-image means automatically generating a corresponding image from a natural language description. Compared with ordinary image generation, text-to-image requires not only visually high-quality images but also correct understanding of the subject, attributes, counts, positions, style and relations between objects in the text. As the field developed, the technical focus shifted from “can an image be generated from text” to “can complex instructions be understood accurately and generation be completed with higher quality, higher efficiency and stronger controllability”.
136: Early text-to-image research was mainly based on generative models such as GAN. The basic method was to encode the text into a vector and feed the text features into the generator as a condition so the result matched the description. This phase proved text-to-image was feasible, but early GAN still had clear limits in complex scene generation, textual semantic understanding and training stability. When a prompt contains several subjects, complex spatial relations or a long description in particular, the model struggles to reproduce all of its semantics accurately. In 2021 OpenAI released DALL·E, which processed text and image Tokens autoregressively with a Transformer, making clear progress in combining complex concepts and controlling attributes and driving the development of large-scale text-to-image models. At the same time diffusion models entered the field. GLIDE combined a text condition with a diffusion model and studied text-guidance methods such as CLIP Guidance and Classifier-Free Guidance, showing that a diffusion model can generate visually high-quality images under text control. In 2022 Google's Imagen further combined the text understanding of large language models with the image generation ability of diffusion models. Imagen uses a pretrained T5 as the text encoder, converts the prompt into a text semantic representation and feeds it into the diffusion model as a condition. The work showed that strengthening the semantic understanding of the text encoder can further improve the agreement between generated images and the text description. With models such as DALL·E, GLIDE and Imagen, text-to-image gradually formed a fairly clear technical flow: text encoder → text semantic representation → diffusion generation model → step-by-step denoising → generated image; and diffusion models, with their good generation quality and training stability, gradually became an important technical route in text-to-image.
138: Early diffusion models usually added and removed noise several times directly in pixel space. As image resolution kept rising, handling a large number of pixels directly brought high training and inference costs. In 2022 Rombach et al. proposed the Latent Diffusion Model (LDM), moving the diffusion process from pixel space into a compressed latent space; see the LDM introduction in 14.4.3. Stable Diffusion's significance is not only that it improved text-to-image quality but that it drove the development of an open-weight text-to-image ecosystem. Around its latent diffusion architecture, many extension techniques emerged, such as LoRA, ControlNet, image-to-image and inpainting, turning text-to-image from plain image generation into a complete visual content production system.
140: Early diffusion models usually used U-Net as the denoising network. Through multi-scale feature extraction and skip connections, U-Net preserves the image's spatial structure well and has long been an important backbone for diffusion models. As generative models kept growing, researchers began exploring Transformer instead of U-Net to get better scaling. In 2022 Peebles and Xie proposed the Diffusion Transformer (DiT), using Transformer in place of the U-Net backbone common in diffusion models. The model first splits the image representation in latent space into several patches, turns them into a Token sequence and then models those Tokens with Transformer. The DiT architecture is shown below:
141: DiT research further showed that the model's compute can be scaled by increasing the Transformer's depth, width and the number of input Tokens. In the original paper's experiments, as compute increased, generation quality tended to keep improving, indicating that the Transformer architecture scales well in diffusion models. DiT's significance is not only replacing U-Net with Transformer but providing a new base architecture for later large-scale image generation models. Since then Transformer gradually became an important technical route for text-to-image models and further developed into multimodal Transformer architectures that handle text and image Tokens together, laying the groundwork for a new generation of text-to-image models such as Stable Diffusion 3 and FLUX.1.
143: As Transformer gradually became an important backbone for text-to-image models, the image generation process itself kept evolving. The DDPM described earlier captures data generation mainly as forward noising, learning the reverse process and step-by-step denoising, while Flow Matching describes the transformation from a simple distribution to the real data distribution in terms of a continuous probability path and a velocity field. In 2024 work related to Stable Diffusion 3 further combined Rectified Flow with Transformer for high-resolution text-to-image. That work proposed the new Multimodal Diffusion Transformer (MMDiT) architecture.
144: Unlike early DiT, which mainly processed image latent Tokens, MMDiT processes text and image representations with separate parameters while using joint attention for information exchange between the two modalities, strengthening the model's understanding of text content, text rendering and complex prompts. FLUX.1, released the same year, continued the route of combining Transformer with Flow Matching. The FLUX.1 series uses a hybrid architecture made of multimodal Transformer Blocks and parallel Diffusion Transformer Blocks and is trained with Flow Matching. The publicly released FLUX.1 model reaches 12B parameters, further showing the trend of Transformer image generation models towards large scale. From this stage on, the technical focus of text-to-image models was no longer limited to improving visual quality but gradually extended to understanding complex prompts, generating text inside images, high-resolution generation, few-step sampling and image editing. Text and images also began entering the Transformer more often as Tokens, with cross-modal information exchange through attention. This shift laid the groundwork for the more efficient and unified multimodal generation models that followed.
146: As text-to-image models grew in scale and quality, practical use began to face new problems. On one hand, large generative models usually need substantial compute and many sampling steps; on the other, real AIGC applications are no longer limited to a single text-to-image task but also need image understanding, image generation, image editing and reference-image generation at the same time. Lowering generation cost and unifying multimodal ability therefore became important directions for text-to-image models.
147: The Z-Image series uses the Scalable Single-Stream Diffusion Transformer (S3-DiT) architecture with 6B parameters. An important feature of S3-DiT is its single-stream architecture: text Tokens, visual semantic Tokens and image VAE Tokens are concatenated along the sequence dimension and fed into one unified Transformer. Compared with dual-stream structures that process modalities separately, this lets different kinds of information interact within a single data flow. Z-Image-Turbo reflects an important direction for modern text-to-image models: keeping strong generation ability while lowering inference cost through model distillation and few-step sampling, making large-scale Transformer image generation models better suited to real deployment.
148: SenseNova-U1.5-8B-MoT moves from text-to-image towards unified multimodality. Besides improving generation efficiency, another important direction is unifying the previously separate multimodal understanding and multimodal generation abilities. SenseNova-U1, released in 2026, proposed the NEO-unify architecture, attempting to achieve multimodal understanding and generation in a single unified model. On that basis SenseNova-U1.5-8B-MoT further strengthens image generation and editing. According to the official release information, the final version of SenseNova-U1.5-8B-MoT was released in August 2026 and further improved instruction following, text and layout generation, native 4K image generation, image editing and visual control.
149: SenseNova-U1.5 builds on the NEO-unify unified multimodal architecture and uses a new image patch encoding and decoding mechanism. The model can not only generate images from a text description but also combine an input image with natural language instructions to do image-to-image, image editing and visual control. This means text-to-image models are gradually developing from a single content generation tool into unified multimodal models that handle understanding and generation together.
